edition: Newton, Principia, Andrew Motte trans., 1729 (Wikisource); Book I, Section III, Proposition XIII; Plate 5, Figure 3.

figures.caption: If a body moves in the perimeter of a parabola, find the law of the centripetal force tending to the focus.

text.latex: Newton has proven the inverse-square law for the \textcolor{parabblue}{ellipse}. Now he treats      the \textcolor{parabblue}{parabola} — the limiting orbit that opens to infinity. A body at $P$      feels a force drawn to the \textcolor{fociorange}{focus $S$}, and \textcolor{radgreen}{$SP$} is the radius      joining them. The question: does this open orbit still yield $F \propto 1/SP^2$?      Newton answers yes, by the same Prop. VI machinery.

Retaining the preceding lemma's construction, let $Q$ be the place into which the body      next succeeds. The \textcolor{constpurple}{standard Prop. VI apparatus} appears: draw $QR$ parallel      to $SP$ and $QT$ perpendicular to $SP$. Then add the parabola-specific ordinate —      \textcolor{constpurple}{$Qv$ parallel to the tangent}, meeting the diameter $PG$ at $v$ and the      distance $SP$ at $x$. These lines let us measure the deflection $QR$ against the geometry      of the curve.

Because triangles $Pxv$ and $SPM$ are similar, and the parabola's focal property makes      the sides $SP$ and $SM$ equal, the corresponding sides $Px$ (that is $QR$) and $Pv$ are      also equal — \textcolor{relgreen}{$QR = Pv$}. Now invoke the conic sections: the square of the      ordinate equals the rectangle of the latus rectum and $Pv$. By Lemma XIII the parabola's      latus rectum is $4PS$, so \textcolor{relgreen}{$Qv^2 = 4PS \cdot Pv = 4PS \cdot QR$}. The curve's      geometry has collapsed cleanly into the focal distance.

As $P$ and $Q$ coincide, the ratio of $Qv$ to $Qx$ becomes a ratio of equality by      Cor. 2 of Lemma VII, so $Qx^2 \to 4PS \cdot QR$. From the similar triangles $QxT$ and      $SPN$, $Qx^2 : QT^2 = PS^2 : SN^2 = PS : SA$, whence \textcolor{resultred}{$QT^2 \propto SP \cdot QR$}.      By Cor. 1 of Prop. VI the force is measured as $1/(SP^2 \cdot QT^2/QR)$, and substituting      gives the \textcolor{resultred}{inverse-square law $F \propto 1/SP^2$}. The parabola obeys the same      law as the ellipse. \textit{Q.E.D.}
